system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2136-06-10 22:00:00 to 2136-06-13 18:42:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male with a history of stroke, tracheostomy, G-tube, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, diabetes, and recurrent infections was admitted for septic shock due to a Proteus mirabilis urinary tract infection. He presented with hypotension, leukocytosis, and acute kidney injury following a blocked Foley catheter. He was treated in the ICU with IV fluids, dopamine, and broad-spectrum antibiotics, then transitioned to ceftriaxone once culture results were available. His renal function and blood pressure normalized, and he was weaned off vasopressors. Pain and neuropsychiatric medications were held initially due to drug interactions but were safely restarted. He improved clinically, completed a course of IV antibiotics, and was discharged to extended care with plans to finish treatment and monitor INR.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, uncontrolled

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I’m Dr. ___ . You were brought in because your feeding tube wasn’t working and you had trouble breathing during transport. I’ll explain everything, and you can nod or shake your head if you understand or have questions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. In the ER, your oxygen dropped, but respiratory therapy suctioned your trach and you improved quickly. We also noticed your trach tube was leaking air, so it needs to be replaced.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods, looks concerned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your urine because your white blood cell count was high. It showed signs of infection — lots of bacteria and white cells. So we’re treating you for a urinary tract infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Raises eyebrows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s not unusual for you given your history. Because you’ve had serious infections before with resistant bacteria, we’re using strong antibiotics — cefepime and daptomycin — through an IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also tried to clear your feeding tube with diet coke in the ER, but it didn’t work. Surgery was consulted, and they recommend replacing it. We’re waiting on a part for your trach exchange too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Slight frown.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s frustrating. But you’re stable, and we’ll get both tubes fixed. For now, you’re on a trach mask and your breathing is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods, relaxes slightly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving — your white count is coming down. The urine culture showed mixed bacteria, likely from contamination, so we’re sticking with broad coverage due to your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your chest X-ray. There’s some opacity in the left lung base — could be atelectasis or mild aspiration. But you’re not feverish or coughing, so we don’t think it’s pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Shakes head — denies cough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So we’ll keep monitoring. Your warfarin was held because your INR was high. We’ll restart it once it’s safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick update — the trach exchange part came in. The respiratory therapist replaced it this morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods — feels okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your breathing sounds clearer. We’ll repeat the chest X-ray to confirm the trach position.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — your GJ tube was evaluated today. It wasn’t completely blocked. The radiologist flushed it with saline and contrast, and it worked fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looks surprised.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes! So we didn’t need to replace it. We restarted your tube feeds. But later, it clogged again briefly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Frowns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: But — we cleared it with diet coke using a 5 cc syringe. That’s important: you must use a 5 cc syringe to generate enough pressure. Smaller ones won’t work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods firmly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your leg pain has been worse, hasn’t it? You’ve been grimacing when we move your legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods — yes, pain in calves and thighs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s neuropathic — nerve pain from your diabetes. So we’re doubling your gabapentin, increasing your fentanyl patch to 200 mcg, and adding a capsaicin cream for your legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods — looks relieved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final update — your white count is down to 11.2, which is much better. Your infection is responding. The chest X-ray shows some atelectasis, but no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back to extended care today. But you need to finish the antibiotics — cefepime and daptomycin — for two more weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Looks concerned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Don’t worry — we placed a PICC line yesterday so you can get IV antibiotics there. And we’ll check your CK weekly — that’s a muscle enzyme — because of daptomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember: use a 5 cc syringe with diet coke daily to prevent clogs. And your warfarin will restart soon — INR check first. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Shakes head — no questions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. We’ll make sure your care team knows all the changes. Get some rest before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line placement went smoothly. The X-ray confirmed it’s in the right spot in the vein. You’re all set for antibiotics at the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — your trach is secure, GJ tube is working, infection is improving, and pain is better managed. Discharge paperwork is ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods — smiles slightly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your usual meds. The new ones are the higher fentanyl patch, more gabapentin, capsaicin cream, and the two IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And — very important — use only a 5 cc syringe to flush the tube. That’s what makes the difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods firmly — understands.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. Transport will arrive soon. Take care, and we’ll follow up with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nods — waves slightly with hand.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male with a history of stroke, tracheostomy, GJ tube, atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, diabetes, and recurrent infections was admitted for a clogged GJ tube, urinary tract infection, and tracheostomy leak. He developed hypoxia during transport due to a mucus plug, which resolved with suctioning. He was treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics—cefepime and daptomycin—due to a history of resistant organisms, despite contaminated urine culture. The tracheostomy was successfully exchanged, and the GJ tube was unclogged using a 5 cc syringe and diet coke. A PICC line was placed for outpatient antibiotic completion. His infection resolved, leg pain was managed with increased gabapentin, fentanyl patch, and capsaicin cream, and he was discharged to extended care with follow-up plans for INR monitoring and CK checks.
